newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain's jobless can fall with radical reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain's jobless can fall with radical reform.

text.p: Spain's unemployment rate on Wednesday dipped to 13.82 percent in December from 14.04 the month before, confirming a steady downtrend, but analysts say labour market reforms are needed to make the rate fall substantially.
"This improvement is a clear effect of the previous reforms ...that should back the government in doing more," said Luca Jellinek, analyst at Paribas Capital market in London.
Spain, plagued by the European Union's highest unemployment rate, is expected to approve more flexible highing and firing policies this year in an effort to reduce joblessness.
In 1994, the previous socialist government approved a reform which introduced temporary jobs, but the conservative Popular Party government intends to introduce more changes.
Reform talks between unions and employers have started and the government has already showed it meant business, threatening to intervene if the change is not radical enough.
"With the likely reform in the labour market we'll see further improvement this year," said Carmen Alcaide, economist at BBV.
"The reform should help especially small- and medium-sized firms to hire people at less rigid conditions," she said.
She forecast that in 1997 the Spanish economy could create around 200,000 new jobs.
In a recently published interview with local press, Spanish Labour Minister Javier Arenas said 237,000 new jobs may be created in 1997.

During 1996, the total number of registered unemployed fell be 16,859. The December data, which declined from the previous December's 15.13 percent, was better than expected, said Borga Garcia Alarco of independent economic group Eriste in Madrid.

"We were expecting a decline of 21,400 (but) we got minus 35,240. January could be against the trend, but right after that we should have constant improvement at least until August," he said, adding he forecast 220,000 new jobs this year.
Instead of spreading inflation worries, the reduction of such high unemployment is typically well received by markets.
"From an investor point of view such a high level of unemployment is a little bit scary," said Paribas' Jellinek.
And with such a weak labour market there are no risks for wage pressure.

"This decline is very good..it came with no upward pression on wages. Unemployment is still high, the job market still weak. A big part of the new jobs seems to came from temporary positions," said Ray Attrill, director of analysis at 4cast in London.

Typically, Spanish analysts give more weight to the quarterly survey by the National Statistics Institute (INE), which is based on sample interviews and registers a far higher rate of unemployment than this one based on the registered number of unemployed.
"What's important now is that both indicators show the same healthy downtrend," said BBV's Alcaide.
In INE's latest quarterly report, unemployment fell 1.59 percent in September to 21.91 percent.
